## Problem

Four rules validate a numeric or length option with a predicate that admits
values no threshold can be built from:

| Rule | Predicate | Admits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `no-spread-text` | `typeof v === 'number'` | `NaN`, `Infinity`, negatives |
| `animation-duration-reasonable` | `!Number.isNaN(parseDurationToSeconds(v))` | negatives (`"-5s"`) |
| `font-size-is-readable` | `Number.isFinite(parseFloat(v))` + unit suffix | negatives (`"-10px"`) |
| `text-spacing-is-readable` | `v.endsWith('em') && Number.isFinite(parseFloat(v))` | negatives (`"-1em"`) |

`line-height-is-vertical-rhythmed` already uses the correct predicate,
`Number.isFinite(v) && v > 0`, so the right pattern exists in the codebase and
is simply applied inconsistently.

## Evidence

Probe against `src/index.js`:

```
a11y/no-spread-text with [true, { maxWidth: NaN }]  on '.a{color:red}'  -> silent, no invalid-option error
a11y/animation-duration-reasonable with [true, { maxDuration: '-5s' }]  -> accepted as valid
```

`NaN` is the damaging one. `characters > NaN` is always `false`, so the
upper bound stops firing entirely, while the `minWidth` bound keeps working —
the rule half-runs. The `minWidth > maxWidth` guard on line 65 does not catch
it either, because `NaN > NaN` is also `false`. A typo in a config silently
removes half a rule with no diagnostic.

A negative `maxDuration` inverts `animation-duration-reasonable`: every
duration exceeds `-5`, so every animated rule is reported.

## Impact

An invalid configuration is accepted as valid and degrades the rule silently.
`utils.validateOptions` exists precisely to fail loudly here.

## Fix

Tighten each predicate to the shape `line-height-is-vertical-rhythmed`
already uses — finite and positive:

- `no-spread-text`: `(v) => Number.isFinite(v) && v > 0`
- `animation-duration-reasonable`: require the parsed seconds to be finite and
  `> 0`
- `font-size-is-readable`: require `parseFloat(v) > 0`
- `text-spacing-is-readable`: require `parseFloat(v) >= 0`

Add a reject case per rule asserting the invalid option produces an
`invalidOption` error rather than being accepted.

## Resolution
All four predicates tightened to finite-and-positive, matching line-height-is-vertical-rhythmed. New src/rules/option-validation.test.js asserts 8 invalid and 5 valid option shapes across the four rules. Convention recorded in arch-profile.md.
title: Option validators accept NaN and negative thresholds, silently disabling the checks

## Problem

`checkInPx` reports a violation when `px % gridPx !== 0`. Zero satisfies the
grid for every grid size, so `line-height: 0px` is accepted. The unitless path
does not have this hole: `checkInRel` compares against `minUnitless`, so
`line-height: 0` is reported.

## Evidence

Probe against `src/index.js`:

```css
.a { line-height: 0; }
```
→ **REPORTED**.

```css
.a { line-height: 0px; }
```
→ **silent**.

Both collapse every line of text onto the same baseline. The rule's own
readability floor catches one spelling and not the other.

## Impact

The rule accepts a value that makes text unreadable, and does so
inconsistently with the unitless form of the identical declaration.

## Fix

Treat a non-positive px line-height as a violation before the grid test:

```js
const checkInPx = (o) => {
  if (!o.value.toLowerCase().endsWith('px')) return false;
  const px = parseFloat(o.value);
  if (!Number.isFinite(px)) return true;
  return px <= 0 || px % gridPx !== 0;
};
```

Add a reject test for `line-height: 0px` alongside the existing `line-height: 0`
case.

## Resolution
checkInPx rejects px <= 0 before the grid test. Unresolvable px values now skip instead of reporting, matching no-spread-text's stated philosophy and fixing an SCSS-variable false positive found while testing. Reject test for 0px, accept test for $base-px.
title: line-height: 0px passes because zero is divisible by the grid

## Problem

The rule reports every `display: none` regardless of the at-rule context it
sits in. Hiding navigation, controls and banners in a print stylesheet is
recommended practice and carries none of the accessibility cost the rule
exists to prevent: print output has no assistive-technology interaction model
in which the hidden node could have been announced.

## Evidence

Probe against `src/index.js`:

```css
@media print { .nav { display: none; } }
```
→ **REPORTED** ("Unexpected using \"{ display: none; }\" in .nav").

Control, unambiguously in scope:

```css
.nav { display: none; }
```
→ REPORTED.

None of the three sources `src/rules/no-display-none/README.md` cites
(CSS-Tricks, A11Y Project, WebAIM) objects to hiding content for print; all
three are about hiding content from screen users while keeping it available to
assistive technology.

## Impact

Every project with a print stylesheet must add a `stylelint-disable` comment,
which then also suppresses genuine violations in the same block.

## Fix

Skip rules whose at-rule ancestry is a print-only media query. Walk
`rule.parent` upward and return early when an `atrule` with `name === 'media'`
has params matching `/\bprint\b/i` and not `\bscreen\b`:

```js
const isPrintOnly = (node) => {
  for (let parent = node.parent; parent; parent = parent.parent) {
    if (parent.type !== 'atrule' || parent.name.toLowerCase() !== 'media') continue;
    const params = parent.params.toLowerCase();
    if (/\bprint\b/.test(params) && !/\bscreen\b/.test(params)) return true;
  }
  return false;
};
```

Add an accept test for `@media print` and a reject test for
`@media screen, print` (which does affect screen output), plus a note in the
rule README.

## Resolution
isPrintOnly walks the at-rule ancestry and skips rules under a print-only media query. @media print and @media only print accepted; @media screen, print and @media screen still reported. Print stylesheets section added to the rule README.
title: no-display-none fires inside @media print, where hiding content is standard practice

body:
## Problem

When a rule declares the same property twice, the later declaration is the one
that applies. Eight rules ignore this: each scans the rule's declarations with
`.some()` and reports if *any* of them matches, regardless of whether that
declaration is overridden by a later one.

The idiom this breaks is the standard CSS fallback — declare a value old
browsers understand, then the modern one that supersedes it. Every such pair
is reported on the strength of the fallback that never applies.

`content-property-no-static-value` has the inverted form of the same bug: its
`.some()` passes the rule when *any* content declaration is acceptable, so a
good declaration masks a bad one that overrides it.

## Evidence

Probes against `src/index.js`. In each pair the first case is correct CSS that
must be silent and is not; the second is the control, which behaves correctly.

| Rule | Reported but overridden |
| --- | --- |
| `no-outline-none` | `.a:focus { outline: none; outline: 1px solid red; }` |
| `no-display-none` | `.a { display: none; display: block; }` |
| `no-text-align-justify` | `.a { text-align: justify; text-align: left; }` |
| `font-size-is-readable` | `.a { font-size: 10px; font-size: 20px; }` |
| `line-height-is-vertical-rhythmed` | `.a { line-height: 1; line-height: 1.6; }` |
| `text-spacing-is-readable` | `.a { color: red; letter-spacing: 0.01em; letter-spacing: 0.2em; }` |
| `animation-duration-reasonable` | `.a { animation-duration: 10s; animation-duration: 1s; }` |
| `no-spread-text` | `.a { color: red; max-width: 20ch; max-width: 60ch; }` |

All eight → **REPORTED**. All eight render exactly as the second value.

The inverted case:

```css
a::before { content: ""; content: "Price: $50"; }
```
`a11y/content-property-no-static-value` → **silent**. `"Price: $50"` is what
renders and what a screen reader may announce — the exact defect the rule
exists to catch.

The most damaging instance is the classic focus-ring fallback, which
`no-outline-none` reports even though the ring is present:

```css
.a:focus { outline: 0; outline: auto 5px Highlight; }
```

## Impact

False positives on a ubiquitous CSS idiom across half the rule set, including
two of the three rules in `recommended.js`. Authors cannot satisfy the rules
without deleting their fallbacks. `content-property-no-static-value` misses
real violations in the same breath.

## Fix

Add a shared helper for the declaration that actually applies, and have each
rule test that one declaration rather than all of them:

```js
// src/utils/declarations.js
export function effectiveDeclaration(node, isTarget) {
  let last = null;
  let important = null;

  for (const child of node.nodes || []) {
    if (child.type !== 'decl' || !isTarget(child.prop.toLowerCase())) continue;
    last = child;
    if (child.important) important = child;
  }

  return important ?? last;
}
```

`!important` is honoured because it beats a later non-important declaration in
the same rule. Where a rule covers a shorthand and its longhands
(`outline`/`outline-style`/`outline-width`, `font`/`font-size`,
`animation`/`animation-duration`), take the last declaration across the whole
family — that is correct for the common ordering in both directions.

Full shorthand-versus-longhand resolution (`outline-style: none` followed by
`outline: 1px solid red`, where the shorthand resets the longhand) is out of
scope; document it as a known limitation rather than building a cascade
engine.

Add a two-case test per rule — overridden-bad-value accepted,
overriding-bad-value rejected — plus both orderings for `content`.

## Resolution
New utils/declarations.js effectiveDeclaration returns the winning declaration (last, !important preferred); all 9 rules rewired through it. Verified all 9 overridden-bad-value cases now silent and all 9 overriding-bad-value controls still report, plus display: none !important followed by display: block. Restructuring made two guards dead (declaredFontSize's non-font branch, animation's else-if chain) and both were deleted rather than tested. Convention recorded in arch-profile.md.
title: Every value rule judges all declarations of a property instead of the one that wins

## Problem

Both counterpart searches — `utils/create-media-query-rule.js` and
`media-prefers-reduced-motion/index.js` — only inspect the offending rule's
direct siblings. A counterpart wrapped in a conditional grouping at-rule is a
nephew, not a sibling, and is invisible to them.

## Evidence

Probes against `src/index.js`, all **REPORTED** and all correct CSS:

```css
a { color: black; }
@supports (color: red) { @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { a { color: white; } } }
```

```css
a { color: black; }
@media screen { @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { a { color: white; } } }
```

```css
.a { animation: spin 1s; }
@layer m { @media (prefers-reduced-motion) { .a { animation: none; } } }
```

The control, both at the same level, is silent:

```css
@layer theme { a { color: black; } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { a { color: white; } } }
```

## Impact

False positives on stylesheets that group their overrides — feature-queried
dark mode, or a media query nested inside a screen query.

## Fix

When scanning following siblings, descend into at-rules that do not change the
cascade origin or layer — `@media`, `@supports`, `@container` — and search
their children recursively for the counterpart.

**Do not descend into `@layer`.** The third probe above is *correctly*
reported: unlayered styles beat every layer, so `.a { animation: spin 1s }`
outside the layer wins over the layered override and no motion is reduced.
Treating `@layer` as transparent would turn a correct report into a false
negative. `@scope` is excluded for the same reason (it changes proximity).

Add accept tests for the `@supports` and nested-`@media` forms, and a reject
test for the `@layer` form that documents why it stays a violation.

## Resolution
targetMediaBlocks descends through media, supports and container at-rules to find the counterpart. @layer and @scope stay opaque by design: unlayered styles beat every layer, so descending would turn a correct report into a false negative. Accept tests for @supports and nested @media; reject test for @layer documenting why it remains a violation.
title: A counterpart inside @supports, @container or a nested @media is not found

## Problem

`isContentPropertyUsedCorrectly` accepts a `content` declaration only when the
selector matches `/:before|:after/`. `::marker` is the third pseudo-element
that legitimately takes `content`, and styling a list bullet through it is
ordinary CSS with no accessibility cost: the marker is presentational, and the
list semantics a screen reader announces come from the list element itself.

## Evidence

Probes against `src/index.js`:

```css
li::marker { content: "- "; }
```
→ **REPORTED** ("Unexpected using \"content\" property in li::marker").

```css
li::marker { content: counter(list-item) ". "; }
```
→ **REPORTED**.

Neither injects text into the accessibility tree in the way `::before` content
can; both are the documented way to restyle a list marker.

## Impact

Restyling a list bullet requires a `stylelint-disable` comment, which then
also suppresses genuine `::before`/`::after` violations in the same rule.

## Fix

Add `::marker` to the pseudo-elements whose `content` is accepted:

```js
const isContentPropertyUsedCorrectly = (selectors) =>
  selectors.every((selector) => /::?(?:before|after|marker)\b/i.test(selector));
```

The anchored form also stops the current pattern matching `:after` inside an
attribute value. Add accept tests for both `::marker` cases above.

## Resolution
::marker is exempt from the value check entirely rather than merely added to the accepted-pseudo list, since any marker content is the bullet glyph. Both regexes anchored on the colon so 'after'/'marker' inside a class or attribute value no longer match. Accept tests for the string and counter forms.
title: content on ::marker is reported, though it only styles the list bullet

## Problem

`.markdownlint.yml` at the repo root configures markdownlint (disabling MD013
and MD043), and `.codacy.yml` excludes only `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/**` and
`**/__tests__/**` — so `README.md` and every rule README are linted. Three
violations are present.

## Evidence

```
$ npx markdownlint-cli2 'src/**/*.md' 'README.md' 'docs/audit/arch-profile.md'
README.md:56 MD040/fenced-code-language Fenced code blocks should have a language specified
src/rules/media-prefers-reduced-motion/README.md:36:28 MD049/emphasis-style Emphasis style [Expected: asterisk; Actual: underscore]
src/rules/media-prefers-reduced-motion/README.md:36:32 MD049/emphasis-style Emphasis style [Expected: asterisk; Actual: underscore]
Summary: 3 issues in 2 files
```

MD049 defaults to "consistent": it takes the first emphasis in a file as the
standard. `media-prefers-reduced-motion/README.md` mixes `*before*` with the
`_not_` phrasing every rule README uses, so that one file is internally
inconsistent while the other fifteen are not.

## Impact

Three avoidable findings on the Codacy dashboard for the project's most
visible file and one rule doc.

## Fix

- `README.md:56` — tag the fence `text`; it holds the bare config string
  `@ivuorinen/stylelint-a11y/recommended`.
- `media-prefers-reduced-motion/README.md:36` — change `*before*` to
  `_before_` to match the `_not_` style already in that file and the other
  fifteen rule READMEs.

## Resolution
README.md fence tagged text; media-prefers-reduced-motion README emphasis changed to underscore to match the file and the other fifteen rule READMEs. markdownlint-cli2 over the Codacy-linted paths is now clean.

## Problem

Finding `audit-790a5234` was fixed by teaching `utils/create-media-query-rule.js`
to descend through `@media`, `@supports` and `@container` when looking for the
counterpart. `media-prefers-reduced-motion` reimplements that search and was
not changed, so the two are out of step again — the precise failure mode
`docs/audit/arch-profile.md` records as the live architectural risk, reproduced
by the fix for the finding that documented it.

## Evidence

Probes against `src/index.js`. The factory-backed rule is correct:

```css
a { color: black; }
@supports (color: red) { @media (prefers-contrast: more) { a { color: white; } } }
```
`a11y/media-prefers-contrast` → silent.

The hand-rolled search is not:

```css
.a { animation: spin 1s; }
@supports (color: red) { @media (prefers-reduced-motion) { .a { animation: none; } } }
```
`a11y/media-prefers-reduced-motion` → **REPORTED**.

```css
.a { animation: spin 1s; }
@media screen { @media (prefers-reduced-motion) { .a { animation: none; } } }
```
→ **REPORTED**.

`@layer` is correctly still reported in both, so only the transparent-at-rule
half is missing.

## Impact

The two rules disagree on identical stylesheet shapes. A project that groups
its overrides gets a false positive from `media-prefers-reduced-motion` — the
rule that matters most, being the only recommended one of the three.

## Fix

Give `overriddenProperties` the same descent. Extract the traversal so both
modules share it rather than adding a third copy: move the transparent-at-rule
set and the block-yielding walk into `utils/`, and have
`create-media-query-rule.js` and `media-prefers-reduced-motion/index.js` both
call it. Add the `@supports` and nested-`@media` accept cases and the `@layer`
reject case to `media-prefers-reduced-motion/__tests__/index.js`.

## Resolution
Extracted the traversal to utils/media-queries.js (featureQueryBlocks + isFeatureQuery + the transparent-at-rule set) and rewired both counterpart searches through it, rather than adding a third copy. media-prefers-reduced-motion now accepts @supports- and nested-@media-wrapped overrides and still reports the @layer case. Regression tests added; arch-profile.md now states that a change to either search must be applied to both or extracted.
title: Grouping-at-rule support landed in only one of the two counterpart searches

## Problem

`create-media-query-rule.js` and `media-prefers-reduced-motion/index.js` both
walk `@page` at-rules and treat `node.params` as a selector, so an `@page`
block declaring a target property is reported. The counterpart search that
would clear the report only matches children of type `rule` — and an `@page`
inside a media query is an `atrule`. There is therefore no CSS an author can
write to satisfy the report.

## Evidence

Probe against `src/index.js`:

```css
@page :first { color: red; }
```
`a11y/media-prefers-color-scheme` → **REPORTED**.

The natural fix a reader would write:

```css
@page :first { color: red; }
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { @page :first { color: white; } }
```
→ still **REPORTED**.

Every `@page` case in all three rules' test files is an `accept` case; not one
`reject` exists, so this report path has never been asserted on.

The feature is also meaningless on its own terms: `prefers-color-scheme`,
`prefers-contrast` and `prefers-reduced-motion` are user-preference features
for interactive media, and `@page` is the printed-page context.

## Impact

An unsatisfiable diagnostic. The only remedy available to an author is a
`stylelint-disable` comment.

## Fix

Delete the `@page` branch from both modules and walk with `root.walkRules`,
the form the other fourteen rules already use. This also removes the
`isStandardSyntaxAtRule` import and the three `@page` guard tests that exist
only to cover it, and closes the "two shapes of the same construct" divergence
`docs/audit/arch-profile.md` has tracked since the first audit round. Update
that profile accordingly.

## Resolution
@page branch deleted from both modules; both now walk with root.walkRules like the other fourteen rules. Removed the isStandardSyntaxAtRule import, the three @page guard tests that existed only to cover it, and five further guards the change made unreachable (nodeless-rule and empty-selector checks, and the isStandardSyntaxSelector call that only ever saw @page params). Accept tests added asserting @page is not walked.
title: The @page branch emits reports no stylesheet can satisfy

## Problem

Rules match property names by exact string, so a vendor-prefixed spelling of a
property they care about is not recognised. Two rules are affected:
`no-important-on-focus` (`isFocusIndicatorProperty`) and
`animation-duration-reasonable` (its animation/transition family predicate).

## Evidence

Probes against `src/index.js`:

```css
.a:focus { -webkit-box-shadow: none !important; }
```
`a11y/no-important-on-focus` → **silent**. The unprefixed control
`box-shadow: none !important` → REPORTED.

```css
.a { -webkit-animation-duration: 10s; }
```
`a11y/animation-duration-reasonable` → **silent**. The unprefixed control
`animation-duration: 10s` → REPORTED.

## Impact

Small. Autoprefixer emits the prefixed property alongside the unprefixed one,
so generated stylesheets are still caught through the standard spelling; only
hand-written legacy CSS that carries the prefix alone slips through.

## Fix

Strip a leading vendor prefix before comparing. One helper beside
`effectiveDeclaration` in `utils/declarations.js`, applied by both rules:

```js
export const unprefixed = (prop) => prop.replace(/^-\w+-/, '');
```

Add a reject test per rule for the prefixed spelling.

## Resolution
Added unprefixed() to utils/declarations.js; no-important-on-focus and animation-duration-reasonable match through it. The report still names the property as written, so -webkit-box-shadow is reported under that name rather than box-shadow.
title: Vendor-prefixed properties are invisible to the property-matching rules

## Problem

`effectiveDeclaration` scans a rule's direct children. A declaration inside an
at-rule nested within the rule is a grandchild, and `root.walkRules` does not
visit the at-rule either — so nothing reaches it. Every value rule therefore
judges the flat and nested spellings of identical CSS differently.

## Evidence

Probes against `src/index.js`. The flat form is reported:

```css
@media screen { .a { display: none; } }
```
`a11y/no-display-none` → REPORTED.

The nested form, which cascades identically, is not:

```css
.a { color: red; @media screen { display: none; } }
```
→ **silent**.

Same for the other value rules:

```css
.a { color: red; @media screen { text-align: justify; } }
```
`a11y/no-text-align-justify` → **silent**.

```css
.a { color: red; @media screen { font-size: 10px; } }
```
`a11y/font-size-is-readable` → **silent**.

A nested *rule* is visited correctly (`root.walkRules` reaches it), so only the
nested at-rule form is blind:

```css
.a { color: red; &:focus { outline: none; } }
```
`a11y/no-outline-none` → REPORTED.

## Impact

False negatives across nine rules on Baseline-available CSS nesting. A
stylesheet migrated from the flat form to the nested form silently loses
coverage, with no diagnostic to say so.

## Fix

A nested conditional at-rule is a separate declaration context: the
declarations in it apply only under that condition, so its effective value must
be resolved within it rather than merged into the rule's. Flattening the
declarations into one list would be wrong — `.a { display: none; @media print
{ display: block } }` is unconditionally `display: none` outside print, and a
naive last-wins scan would call it `block`.

Add to `utils/declarations.js`:

```js
export function* declarationContexts(rule) {
  yield rule;

  for (const child of rule.nodes) {
    if (child.type === 'atrule' && child.nodes) yield* declarationContexts(child);
  }
}

export const someContext = (rule, violates) => {
  for (const context of declarationContexts(rule)) {
    if (violates(context)) return true;
  }

  return false;
};
```

Each value rule then wraps its existing per-rule check in `someContext` and
takes the context rather than the rule. `no-display-none`'s `isPrintOnly` walks
`parent` upward, so it keeps working per context and the `@media print` case
stays exempt. Reporting stays on the rule node, so messages are unchanged.

Add a nested-form reject case per rule, and a `@media print` accept case for
`no-display-none`.

## Resolution
Added declarationContexts/someContext to utils/declarations.js and routed all nine value rules through them, so a nested at-rule is judged as its own context rather than merged or skipped. isPrintOnly now starts at the node itself so a nested @media print context stays exempt. Verified the nested spelling now reports for all nine rules, that .a { display: block; @media print { display: none } } stays silent, and that .a { display: none; @media print { display: block } } still reports.
title: Declarations inside a nested at-rule are invisible, so the nested spelling of a violation is not checked

## Problem

`outlineProperties` covers `outline`, `outline-style` and `outline-width`, but
not `outline-color`. A transparent outline colour makes the ring invisible just
as surely as a zero width — and the rule already understands that `transparent`
does not count, since it rejects a `transparent` border or box-shadow as a
replacement.

## Evidence

Probe against `src/index.js`:

```css
.a:focus { outline: 2px solid; outline-color: transparent; }
```
→ **silent**. The focus ring is invisible.

The control confirms the rule is otherwise looking:

```css
.a:focus { outline: 2px solid; outline-color: red; }
```
→ silent, correctly.

## Impact

A focus indicator can be removed through `outline-color` with no diagnostic,
in the rule whose entire purpose is to catch removed focus indicators. It is
in `recommended.js`.

## Fix

Add `outline-color` to `outlineProperties`, and give `removesOutline` a branch
for it:

```js
if (prop === 'outline-color') return parts[0] === 'transparent';
```

Note this joins the shorthand family for `effectiveDeclaration`, which is
correct: `outline: 2px solid red` after `outline-color: transparent` resets the
colour.

Add a reject test for the transparent case and an accept test for a real
colour.

## Resolution
outline-color added to outlineProperties with a transparent branch in removesOutline. Joining the family also means a later outline shorthand correctly resets an earlier transparent colour. Reject test for transparent, accept test for a real colour.
title: outline-color: transparent hides the focus ring without being detected

`obsoleteElements` holds 28 of the 29 elements in the WHATWG HTML

## Problem

Both counterpart searches accept an override only when its selector list is
*identical* to the offending rule's (`normalizeSelector(a) === normalizeSelector(b)`).
Coverage is the actual requirement: an override written for
`.card:hover, .card:focus` applies to every element `.card:hover` applies to,
so it neutralises that rule.

Because equality is demanded instead, a broader override is invisible, the rule
reports again, and `--fix` inserts a *second* override. The next pass inserts a
third. `--fix` never converges.

This becomes reachable as soon as another fixable rule widens a selector —
`selector-pseudo-class-focus` rewriting `.card:hover` to
`.card:hover, .card:focus` does exactly that, including inside a
reduced-motion block.

## Evidence

Probe against `src/index.js` with `selector-pseudo-class-focus` and
`media-prefers-reduced-motion` both enabled, `fix: true`, on:

```css
.card:hover { animation: slide 12s ease 2s infinite; }
```

Pass 1 inserts the override and widens the selector inside it:

```css
@media screen and (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
.card:hover, .card:focus { animation: none;
}
}
```

Pass 2 does not recognise that override as covering `.card:hover`, and appends
another:

```css
@media screen and (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
.card:hover, .card:focus { animation: none;
}
.card:hover { animation: none;
}
}
```

Each rule in isolation is idempotent; only the combination diverges, which is
why the per-rule `fixed:` assertions did not catch it.

## Impact

`--fix` is non-convergent with the recommended config. Every run of
`stylelint --fix` on a stylesheet with a hovered, animated rule grows the file
by one duplicate override block — unbounded growth in a pre-commit hook.

## Fix

Match on coverage rather than equality. Add to `utils/selectors.js`:

```js
export function coversSelectors(candidate, required) {
  const have = new Set(candidate.split(',').map((part) => part.trim()));

  return required
    .split(',')
    .map((part) => part.trim())
    .every((part) => have.has(part));
}
```

Use it for the three "is this the counterpart for that rule" comparisons — in
`utils/create-media-query-rule.js`, and in `overriddenProperties` and
`addOverrides` in `media-prefers-reduced-motion/index.js`. A narrower override
still fails to cover a broader rule, which is correct.

Add a cross-rule convergence case to `src/rules/autofix-safety.test.js`: fix
with every fixable rule enabled, twice, and assert the second pass is a no-op.

## Resolution
Replaced normalizeSelector equality with coversSelectors (subset test) at all three counterpart comparisons. normalizeSelector became unused and was deleted. Verified convergent over 6 --fix passes under both the full rule set and recommended.js, and that a narrower override still correctly fails to cover a broader rule. Cross-rule convergence case added to autofix-safety.test.js — the per-rule fixed: assertions could not have caught this because each rule is idempotent alone.
